prediction:
THOUGHT: This 58-year-old female developed acute, watery diarrhea (≥9 episodes in 2 days) with lower abdominal cramping and diffuse mild lower abdominal tenderness shortly after initiation of levofloxacin for community-acquired pneumonia. She has no fever, no vomiting, no hematochezia, and no recent travel or dietary changes — making infectious causes unrelated to antibiotics (e.g., Salmonella, Campylobacter, norovirus) less likely. Crucially, she received a broad-spectrum fluoroquinolone (levofloxacin), a well-established risk factor for Clostridioides difficile infection (CDI). CDI typically presents with antibiotic-associated watery diarrhea, abdominal cramping, and leukocytosis — all present here (WBC 13,400/mm³ with 80% neutrophils; ESR elevated at 33 mm/hr, consistent with inflammatory response). Physical exam shows no signs of peritoneal irritation or sepsis, supporting uncomplicated CDI rather than fulminant colitis. Although stool C. difficile toxin testing is not yet reported, the clinical context — recent antibiotic exposure, acute onset, high stool frequency, abdominal discomfort, and inflammatory lab findings — makes CDI the overwhelmingly most likely diagnosis. Other considerations (e.g., osmotic diarrhea from medications, viral gastroenteritis) are far less probable given the temporal association with levofloxacin and absence of alternative exposures.

DIAGNOSIS: Clostridioides difficile infection
